questions.question: Why did people start using money instead of just trading things?
options: Because they enjoyed collecting shiny objects.
To make buying and selling goods easier.
Because kings back then forbade people from trading.
Because money can be used better for building houses.
questions.explanation: Money was invented as a tool to simplify trade compared to the complex barter system.

questions.question: Who agreed that money has value?
options: Only the shopkeepers in candy stores.
Scientists who invented a special kind of paper.
People in society, so they could trade together.
Children who wanted something colorful in their wallets.
questions.explanation: Money works because society collectively agrees and trusts that it represents value.

questions.question: In what forms can we find money today?
options: Only as coins and paper banknotes in a wallet.
As coins, banknotes, or digital money on a card.
Only as gold bars kept in a bank.
As colorful stickers that we swap at school.
questions.explanation: Modern money exists in physical forms (cash) and digital forms (bank accounts/cards).

questions.question: What gives an ordinary coin its real value?
options: The fact that it is made of a very rare type of metal.
People's agreement that coins serve as a means of payment.
The fact that it has the year of production stamped on it.
Its round shape, which prevents it from getting stuck.
questions.explanation: A coin's value comes from its social function as an accepted currency, not the metal itself.

questions.question: Chrumko is holding a 2-euro coin. What can he do with it in a shop?
options: He must return it because it is just a worthless piece of metal.
He can exchange it for goods worth two euros.
He cannot buy anything at all with a 2-euro coin.
He must clean it at home first for it to have any price.
questions.explanation: The coin is a valid tool for purchasing items up to its face value.

questions.question: What would happen in a shop if money did not exist?
options: All things would be free for every person.
We would have to carry our things and trade them.
Shops would not exist and we would make everything ourselves.
Shopkeepers would give us things in exchange for poems.
questions.explanation: Without money, we would revert to a barter system where physical items are swapped.

questions.question: Why is direct trading (barter) sometimes very difficult?
options: Because nobody wants any things at all.
The other person might not want what you are offering.
Because trading things is forbidden by new laws.
Because things always break or get ruined during a trade.
questions.explanation: Barter requires a 'coincidence of wants'—both parties must want exactly what the other has.

questions.question: What is the main role of money when buying a snack?
options: It serves as a tool for a quick and fair exchange.
It helps us calculate how many calories an apple has.
It makes our school bag much heavier.
It ensures that our snack tastes much better.
questions.explanation: Money acts as a medium of exchange that everyone accepts, making transactions fast.

questions.question: What does it mean that money is 'universal'?
options: That it can be used throughout the whole galaxy.
That everyone will accept it in exchange for goods.
That it can be washed in a washing machine without being ruined.
That it always has exactly the same color.
questions.explanation: Universal means it is widely accepted by everyone in a society as payment.

questions.question: Chrumko has an apple but wants a snack bar. His friend has a bar but doesn't want the apple. How to solve this?
options: Chrumko must convince his friend to take the apple anyway.
Chrumko can buy the bar with money, which everyone wants.
Chrumko must eat the apple and stay hungry.
They must go to the teacher to have her divide the things.
questions.explanation: Money solves the problem of mismatched needs in a direct trade.

questions.question: Imagine you want a bike and have 100 kilos of potatoes to trade. Why is it better to have money?
options: Money doesn't take up much space and doesn't rot.
Nobody wants potatoes.
Money is nicer to look at than a sack of potatoes.
The bike seller definitely has an allergy to potatoes.
questions.explanation: Money is portable and serves as a 'store of value' unlike perishable goods like potatoes.

lessons.lessonName: How people paid in the past

questions.question: What is the exchange of things without using money called?
options: Inflation
Investing
Barter
Loan
questions.explanation: Barter is the historical method of exchanging goods directly for other goods.

questions.question: What did people use for payment before coins existed?
options: Paper banknotes
Things like salt, shells, or metal
Only digital money
Exclusively gold bars
questions.explanation: Before standardized coins, people used 'commodity money'—useful items like salt or rare shells.

questions.question: Why was paying in the past more complicated than today?
options: Because people did not have any shops
Because there was no food available
They had to find things to trade that the other person wanted
Because everything cost way too much
questions.explanation: Direct exchange required finding a specific person who wanted your specific item.

questions.question: What was created only after the period of barter and paying with objects?
options: The first coins
Credit cards
Internet banking
Paper money
questions.explanation: Standardized metal coins were the first major step away from barter.

questions.question: Chrumko wants bread, but he doesn't have the eggs that the baker wants. What must he do?
options: Wait until the baker changes his mind
Find someone who will give him bread for free
Find eggs first so he can trade them
Go to a different city
questions.explanation: In a barter system, if you don't have what the seller wants, you cannot complete the trade.

questions.question: Why did people stop using barter as the main way of paying?
options: Because barter trade was too simple and inefficient for society back then.
Because most objects at that time suddenly lost their value.
Because it was hard to find someone who wanted your goods and offered what you needed.
Because trading was officially banned by new royal decrees.
questions.explanation: Barter is inefficient because it is rare for two people to perfectly match their supply and demand.

questions.question: What do coins, banknotes, and money on a card have in common?
options: They are different forms of the same money we use to pay.
We have to print all these forms of money at home before shopping.
They are made of the same material so they always weigh the same.
They only work if we show them all at once to the shopkeeper.
questions.explanation: Regardless of appearance, they all represent the same value used for transactions.

questions.question: What does it mean to pay in cash?
options: Paying by card over the internet
Paying with coins or banknotes
Sending money through a mobile app
Paying only with very large banknotes
questions.explanation: Cash refers specifically to physical currency like coins and paper bills.

questions.question: Where is digital money located?
options: In a wallet
In the bank as gold bars
In a bank account
In the shop at the cash register
questions.explanation: Digital money is a record of value stored electronically in a bank's system.

questions.question: What happens when you pay with a card in a shop?
options: Money physically moves from the wallet to the cash register
Money is sent digitally from the account
Your payment card is completely erased right after paying.
The bank sends new coins to your home by mail for every payment.
questions.explanation: Card payments trigger an electronic transfer between the buyer's and seller's bank accounts.

questions.question: Chrumko paid for a tie with banknotes and coins. What payment method did he use?
options: Digital payment
Installment plan
Cash
Exchange (barter)
questions.explanation: Physical money (coins and notes) is always categorized as cash.

questions.question: Chrumko wants to pay for the tie in cash. What must he do?
options: He must hand physical banknotes or metal coins to the shopkeeper.
He must tap his mobile phone on the payment terminal.
It is enough if he promises the shopkeeper to bring the money later.
He must leave his payment card in the shop as a guarantee.
questions.explanation: Cash payments require the physical transfer of currency.

questions.question: Chrumko pays for his purchase with a mobile phone. What does this mean?
options: He used digital money from his account
He paid in cash through the phone
He will pay the money only later
He exchanged goods for other goods
questions.explanation: Mobile payments are a way to access and send digital money.

questions.question: The shopkeeper asked Chrumko if he wants to pay by card or in cash. Why did she give him a choice?
options: Because the tie will cost much more money if he pays by card.
Because both options are correct ways to pay for goods.
Because cash can only be used to buy things that are blue.
Because if he pays in cash, the shopkeeper can keep the money.
questions.explanation: Modern shops usually accept both physical and digital payments as they have the same value.

questions.question: Why can you buy more for 10 euros than for 1 euro?
options: Because 10 euros has a higher value than 1 euro
Because 1 euro is older
Because 10 euros is prettier
Because 1 euro cannot be used in a shop
questions.explanation: Higher numbers on currency represent greater purchasing power.

questions.question: Do all coins and banknotes have the same value?
options: Yes, every coin in the shop works exactly the same regardless of the number.
No, each coin and banknote represents a different amount of money.
It depends on whether it is nice outside or raining; then the value changes.
Only if they are the same size and have the same silver color.
questions.explanation: Currency is denominated into different amounts to allow for precise payments.

questions.question: Which of the following has a greater value?
options: 50 cents
1 euro
20 cents
150 cents
questions.explanation: 150 cents is equal to 1.50 euros, which is more than the other options.

questions.question: Chrumko sees the number 50 on a coin and also on a banknote. What is true?
options: Both have the same value because the same number is written on them.
The coin has a higher value because it is made of metal and is heavier.
The banknote has a much higher value because 50 euros is more than 50 cents.
Neither thing has any value until Chrumko puts sugar on it.
questions.explanation: You must look at the unit (cents vs euros); 50 euros is 100 times more than 50 cents.

questions.question: Chrumko has 1 euro. Juice costs 90 cents and a cookie costs 50 cents. What is true?
options: He can buy both things
He cannot buy either thing
He can buy only one of them
He can buy both things and still have money left
questions.explanation: Total cost (1.40) is more than 1 euro, so he can only afford one item.

questions.question: Chrumko has 2 euros. Juice costs 90 cents and a cookie costs 50 cents. How much will he have left?
options: 60 cents
40 cents
1 euro
10 cents

questions.question: What must Chrumko do if he wants to buy both juice and a cookie but doesn't have enough money?
options: He must choose only one thing or save up more money.
He should take the things and leave the shop without paying.
He should wait until the prices in the shop disappear on their own.
He must break the cookie in half so that it costs less money.
questions.explanation: When money is limited, you must prioritize or save for the future.

questions.question: What happens when you spend all your money?
options: The money will reappear in your wallet on its own by morning.
You won't be able to buy anything else until you get new money.
The shop must give you everything for free since you bought a lot already.
Your wallet will start glowing to warn you that you should go shopping.
questions.explanation: Money is a finite resource; once used, it is gone from your possession.

questions.question: Why is it important to think about what we spend money on?
options: Because money is infinite
So that we have money for other things later
Because spending is forbidden
To have the heaviest wallet possible
questions.explanation: Budgeting ensures you can afford essentials and save for future goals.

questions.question: What does it mean that money is not infinite?
options: That we always have enough of it
That we can never spend it all
That we only have a limited amount
That it only exists in a bank
questions.explanation: Everyone has a budget limit based on what they earn or receive.

questions.question: What should Chrumko do next time he gets money?
options: Spend it all at once
Hide it and never use it
Spend part of it and save part of it
Give it all to his friends
questions.explanation: Balancing spending and saving is the key to healthy money management.

questions.question: Chrumko has 5 euros and spends them on sweets. What is true?
options: He still has money for a toy
He no longer has money for another thing
He can buy even more sweets
The money will come back to him
questions.explanation: By spending his entire budget on one category, he has nothing left for others.

questions.question: Chrumko saves 2 euros out of 5 euros. How much does he have left to spend?
options: 5 euros
3 euros
2 euros
7 euros
questions.explanation: 5 (total) - 2 (saved) = 3 (available to spend).

questions.question: How do people most often get money?
options: They find it randomly on the street
For the work they perform
By printing it at home
By trading it for toys
questions.explanation: Work is the primary source of income for most adults.

questions.question: What is the reward for work called?
options: Gift
Prize
Salary or wage
Fine
questions.explanation: A salary or wage is the official term for money earned through employment.

questions.question: What does it depend on how much money a person earns?
options: On the color of their clothes
On the weather
On the job, time, and experience
On how many friends they have
questions.explanation: Income levels are usually determined by skills, hours worked, and the type of role.

questions.question: Where does money for work most often arrive today?
options: In cash from hand to hand
To a bank account
To school
To the shop
questions.explanation: Most modern employers pay employees via digital bank transfers.

questions.question: Chrumko's mom goes to work and gets money in her account. What will the family use it for?
options: Only for toys
For housing, food, and other necessary things
Only for sweets
They won't use it at all
questions.explanation: Earned income is primarily used to cover living expenses (needs) before wants.

questions.question: How do children most often get money?
options: By daily work in a job
By earning it through business
As an allowance or as a gift
From their parents' bank account without permission
questions.explanation: Children usually receive money through gifts or allowances from their guardians.
